Tick (manual, 2026-08-22) — **recurrence and period**
(`Survival/ClearRecurrence.lean`, new green module, 12 theorems,
base-axiom-clean, no warnings). The structural statistics of an immortal
solver, all off the same ledger. **`count_mod_ten`**: occupancy `≡ 4n (mod 10)`
— clears move mass in units of 10, so the residue is a clock and only 21 of the
201 cell counts are available at any moment. **`five_dvd_of_count_eq`**: if the
board ever returns to a previous cell count, the window between the visits
cleared at EXACTLY 2.8/bag (zero error) and its length is a multiple of 5.
**`exists_count_eq_le`**: by pigeonhole every 201 placements contains such an
exact-balance window — the 2.8 rate is attained on the nose at bounded
intervals, not merely in the limit; `exists_recurrent_count` upgrades this to
"some occupancy recurs infinitely often". **`bag_card_trace`**: under legal
draws the bag holds `7 − n%7` pieces, a mod-7 clock. Combining the two clocks,
**`thirtyfive_dvd_of_trace_eq`: every closed cycle in the state graph has length
divisible by 35 placements = 5 bags** — an arithmetic lower bound on any M2
certificate with no geometry, no reachability and no search. Independent
confirmation of the 5-bag lattice that `perfect_rectangle_bag_period_even` and
the zone-rate/tessellation analyses reached separately. Next: sharpen the
pigeonhole constant 201 → ~101 via `count_mod_ten`; push `35 ∣ Δn` into
`ClosedCycle`/`AdversarialClosedCycle` so it constrains the M2 artifact itself.

Tick (manual, 2026-08-21b) — **the deviation calculus**
(`Survival/ClearDeviation.lean`, new green module, 21 theorems,
base-axiom-clean, no warnings). Quantifies the drift the 2.8 law permits. Core:
`deficit n = 4n − cols·cleared n` and **`deficit_eq_mass`** — the deficit IS the
board occupancy, so it is confined to `[0,200]` forever. Readings: (1)
**uniform window bound** — over ANY `w`-bag window the clears land within 20
rows of `2.8w`; one 20-row budget shared across every time scale. (2)
**`centered_nonpos`** — a solver is never AHEAD; surplus cannot be banked, so
"clear extra now, spend later" is not a strategy that exists. (3) **the
shortfall hyperbola** `sustained_shortfall_window_le`: a shortfall of β rows/bag
survives at most `20/β` bags; contrapositive `lost_of_sustained_shortfall` is
the predictive death-horizon test. (4) **`lost_of_dry_spell`** — 8 bags deliver
224 > 200 cells, so no solver goes eight bags without clearing; seven is the
hard max. (5) `bagClears_le_twentytwo` — per-bag clears ∈ {0..22}, so the
MARGINAL variance is unconstrained; the real constraint is on the LONG-RUN
variance, which `centered_sq_div_tendsto_zero` shows is exactly 0. (6)
**`covariance_sum_le`** — with no dependence assumption the whole `m×m`
covariance matrix sums to ≤ 400, so the autocovariances must cancel the marginal
variance completely; specialized, **`survival_forces_indep_variance_zero`**:
independent per-bag clearing with any spread whatsoever is fatal. Honest limit:
the deterministic certificates fire exactly at death, never strictly before, so
prediction requires an extrapolation hypothesis. Next: per-lag autocorrelation
bounds; couple the dry-spell bound to `perfect_rectangle_bag_period_even`.

Tick (manual, 2026-08-21) — **the clearing-rate law**
(`Survival/ClearRate.lean`, new green module, base-axiom-clean, no warnings).
Formalizes the "≥2.8 rows cleared per bag is needed for infinite play"
folklore and settles it: the rate is pinned from BOTH sides, so the answer is
an equality, not an inequality. `mass_ledger`/`init_ledger` give conservation
along a policy trace (`board.count + cols·cleared = 4·placements`), which makes
the clearing deficit *literally* the board mass. Hence `bags_sandwich`:
`2.8m − 20 ≤ cleared ≤ 2.8m` — floor from the ≤200-cell capacity of a live
board, ceiling because a row must be filled before it can be cleared (equality
iff perfect clear, `cleared_eq_iff_board_empty`). Consequences:
**`lost_of_clear_deficit`** (a boardful behind ⇒ already lost — a finite death
certificate), **`survival_forces_clear_rate`** (`bagRate → 2.8`, squeeze),
**`not_survivesForever_of_rate_lt`** (eventually `≤ 2.8 − ε` ⇒ tops out), and
`not_rate_ge_add` (`2.8 + ε` is unreachable at ANY horizon). `play_bag_sandwich`
restates it policy-free over arbitrary placement lists (covers adversarial
solvers); `average_clears_bounds` / `expected_clears_bounds` push it through
finite averages and arbitrary probability measures. Interpretation: 2.8 is a
CONSERVATION LAW, not a budget to beat — the open problem is the geometry of
cashing the drains, never the rate arithmetic (cf. `BagBurst`'s
`drain_budget_ge_clearing_need`). Next tick: burstiness/variance bounds forced
by the 7-bag, and combine the rate window with
`perfect_rectangle_bag_period_even` to bound how often immortal play can sit at
a perfect clear.

Tick (manual, 2026-07-27b) — **the traveling-wave design: the coupled 9-column
schedule as bouncing staircases** (design tick; arithmetic hand-verified
against the LaneCalculus update laws, no Lean this tick). The coupled cycle's
architecture: the surface is flats (plateaus/plains) separated by 3-level
RIGID STAIRCASES `[plateau k+2 | stair k+1 | plain k]` = the waves. VERIFIED
exactly: (1) TRANSLATION — one `place_horizZ_step` at the stair advances a
descending (S-)staircase 2 columns right, raising the 2 passed columns +2
(mirror: `place_horizS_step` moves ascending staircases left); a 9-col sweep
is 4 pushes. (2) REFLECTION — at the right wall `place_stepT_toZ` (T1) turns
an arriving S-staircase into a departing Z-staircase in one move (T3 mirror at
the left wall); the wall column gains +3 and the ladder climbs +2 per bounce.
(3) ABSORPTION — two converging fronts at plain-width 1 form the exact notch
and `place_notchT` (T0) merges the plateaus into a full flat (a completed
+2 layer); plain width changes by 2 per push, so width parity is invariant:
collisions can be SCHEDULED to always land at width 1. (4) EMISSION is the
delicate step: a bare `place_flatT_lane` (T2) bump sits one level above the
plain and cannot propagate until flanked — fronts only translate at matched
elevations; emissions must be built where plateau levels already agree.
Piece roles: S/Z fuel opposite-direction fronts; T alternates reflect/absorb/
emit (T-parity ✓); O/L/J run the pair economy on the wide flats between wave
passes (keeping plateau/plain levels aligned is a scheduling constraint, ≤2-bag
pair cycles vs 2-col/bag wave speed); band-I = `place_horizI_lane` on a flat-4
plain. THE REMAINING OPEN DESIGN QUESTION, now sharp: PHASING — every bag
delivers one S and one Z, so at every bag boundary the family must present
both an S-eater (descending front with right runway, or reflectable) and a
Z-eater (ascending front with left runway); a single bouncing wave fails
(during a rightward leg the arriving S has no receptor: vS on the front breaks
rigidity). Candidate: two anti-phase waves with staggered reflections, with
the T budget (1 per bag) shared between reflections and absorb/emit events.
Next tick: solve the phasing/order table (state = front positions+directions ×
bag remainder), then discharge PlinthCert's schedule obligations from the
LaneCalculus laws.

Tick (manual, 2026-07-27) — **the lane calculus: the complete local flush
transition pack** (`Invariants/LaneCalculus.lean`, 15 place theorems + 9 drop
profiles, all via `place_flush_skyline`, base-axiom-clean, lint-clean). Every
flush landing shape in the slot algebra now has its skyline transition law at
ARBITRARY surrounding profiles: horizontal S on `(k,k,k+1)` / horizontal Z on
`(k+1,k,k)` (the 3-wide step lanes), the three notch fills (T0/L2/J2 → local
flat), the T alternator T1/T3 at general profiles, local flat-3 (T2/L0/J0) and
flat-4 (I) landings, and the L/J pair economy (L1/J3 flat→±2, L3/J1 ±2→flat).
KEY DESIGN FINDINGS toward the coupled 9-column cycle (hand analysis, exact in
the new lemmas): (1) the S/Z/T trio is order-robust on three standing ±1 pairs
and PROVABLY NOT on two — but three standing pairs are rate-dead (2/bag/col vs
2.8 required, and ±1 pairs cannot receive O/L/J mass by `sStep_exclusive`) ⇒
roving receptors are FORCED, the design-level rediscovery of rate coupling.
(2) THE ROVING STEP: `place_horizZ_step` on a standing S-window plus a runway
column at the low height FLATTENS the window and re-emits it one column right
(mirror: `place_horizS_step`) — the flattening move the redirect puzzle was
missing; ±1 receptors can now migrate and their columns can then take O/L/J
mass. (3) Verified flat-to-flat lane cycles (+4 rows on a 3-lane, exact lemma
chains): A_S = L0·Sh·L2 ({S,2L}), A_Z = J0·Zh·J2 ({Z,2J}), C_T = T2·T3·L3
({2T,L}), F = {O,L,J} in both landing orders (L0·O·J2 and J0·O·L2), E_I =
vI·O·O ({I,2O}). REMAINING OPEN (next tick): the cross-bag phase machine —
compose the cycle primitives into a family closed under adversarial within-bag
order at matched rates (supply {S,Z,T,O,L,J} + 0.3 band-I per bag vs the
cycles' piece demands; the O-first flat-availability invariant is the sharpest
constraint), then discharge PlinthCert's schedule obligations from it.

Tick (manual, 2026-07-12) — **FINDINGS D1/D2 + the plinth foundation**.
D1: `ShiftCertificate`/`BandScheduleCert` (2026-07-09/10) are SOUND but
UNINHABITABLE — every placement obligation propagates the base unchanged, the
drain lowers it, `initBase` starts at 0: the drain guard `4 ≤ b` is unreachable,

re-anchoring, the forced row-0 bootstrap hole (any first S/Z on flat) blocks all
re-anchors (`holeLift` row arithmetic) — physically, a row-0 hole means rows 0–3
are never simultaneously full. FIX (the plinth): one bag-1 J-rot-3 placement
plugs the well's row 0 (`place_wellPlug_flat`); row 0 becomes a permanent floor
whose hole keeps it from ever clearing (`fullRows_plinth_eq_empty` — the floor
is immortal); drains fill and clear rows 1–4 (`drain_debtBoard_plinthLift`,
a MID-ROW clear proven from the raw `clearLines`); the band rides `c + 1` above
in coordinates the hole never touches, so re-anchoring (`ReanchorsTo`) is free.

BARE skyline reps — all mechanisms reuse, T2′, the plug) +
`Safety/PlinthCert.lean` (`PlinthMem` re-anchored membership, two-regime

layout well+S+Z+T+OLJ = 10; the redirect flush-compatibility puzzle) in

Tick 1915 (cron, 2026-06-05) — **Cycle-side
`solverReachable` ⇒ `Reachable`**:

1. `AdversarialClosedCycle.solverReachable_reachable`:
   `init ∈ C.states → solverReachable C.solver g →
   Reachable cfg g`.

**Proof**: induction on `solverReachable hg`.
- `init`: `Reachable.init`.
- `@step g' p hsr hp ih`: derive mem-states /
  not-lost / valid via `C.solverReachable_mem_states`
  / `C.not_lost` / `C.solver_valid_and_piece`,
  build the `Placement` eta equality
  `{ C.solver g' p with piece := p } = C.solver g'
  p` via `rcases`+`cases hpiece`+`rfl`, then apply
  `ih.adversarialStep hnl hp` with the eta-rewritten
  validity. Mirrors `adversarialTrace_reachable_of_init`.

**Why substantive (per user pivot — fundamental
solverReachable→Reachable bridge)**:

The single most important cycle-side bridging
lemma between the inductive `solverReachable`
predicate (init-rooted, cycle-solver-driven) and
the general `Reachable cfg` predicate (init-rooted,
any-legal-placement-driven). All previous
trace-level Reachable lemmas were specialised to
particular trace sequences; this one works for
*any* solverReachable state.

The proof uses `C.valid` essentially: without it,
`solverReachable C.solver g` would not imply
`Reachable cfg g` (because Reachable requires
`Placement.Valid`, which is only guaranteed by
the cycle structure). This is precisely the
`SolvesTetrisValid`-analog for cycles —
`solverReachable_reachable_of_solvesTetrisValid`
(Adversarial.lean ~3036) is the
SolvesTetrisValid-side; this is the cycle-side.

|---|---|---|
| `SolvesTetrisValid` | `SolvesTetrisValid cfg σ` | `solverReachable_reachable_of_solvesTetrisValid` (~3036) |
| Cycle | `init ∈ C.states` | **1915 (this)** |

**Operational consequence**: now any solverReachable
state can be converted to `Reachable cfg g`. This
enables `inFieldStates` embedding, board well-formedness,
and all M3-style reachability proofs for cycle-derived
solverReachable states.

**Goal-alignment**:
- (M3 — Reachable cycles): direct

artifact equality at the data-field level. The

`M.atlas = M'.atlas` and `M.states = M'.states`

| ↔ | Use M = M' as a pair of facts (and vice versa) | `eq_iff` (this) |

The `eq_iff` form is particularly useful for
substituting M-equality assumptions in `simp`/`rw`
chains — extracting both atlas and states
equalities in one step.

**decidable refinement** of atlas equality +
states equality. Any algorithmic check needing
to confirm or refute M4 equality reduces to two
independent checks.

Tick 1769 (cron, 2026-06-05) — **`M.canon` trace
equals `M` trace**: adversarial trace under canon
solver = adversarial trace under original solver.

Added in `Proofs/SafeSet.lean` right after Tick
1725's `toSolver_trace_full_invariants_of_init`:

1. `AdversarialClosedCycle.M4Artifact.adversarialTrace_canon_eq_self`:
   for any M4 artifact M and legal piece sequence,
   `adversarialTrace cfg M.canon.atlas.toSolver s
    GameState.init n = adversarialTrace cfg M.atlas.toSolver
    s GameState.init n` at every step.

**Proof strategy** (induction on n):
- Base (n = 0): both = init, rfl.
- Step (n = k+1):
  1. `adversarialTrace_succ` on both sides exposes
     the step-form.
  2. `rw [ih]` substitutes trace_canon k → trace_orig k.
  3. Extract `hg : trace_orig k ∈ M.states` via
     Tick 1722's trace mem-states.
  4. Extract `hp : s k ∈ trace_orig k.bag` via
     `LegalSequence.canDraw` + `adversarialTrace_bag`.
  5. Apply Tick 1766's `canon_atlas_toSolver_eq_at_active`
     to equate the canon and original solver values.

**Why substantive (per user pivot — trace agreement
under canonicalization)**:

This is a **strong trace identity**:

> **Theorem**: For any M4 artifact M and legal
> piece sequence, the entire adversarial trace
> under canon's materialised solver is bit-
> identical to the trace under original's

**Proof**: `unfold Solver.toAtlas` exposes the

Combined with Tick 1714, this characterises both
sides of the Solver ↔ Atlas correspondence:

| Direction | Statement | Tick |
|---|---|---|

| Atlas round-trip | `A g p = some pl → A.toSolver.toAtlas g p = some pl` (partial, only when defined) | 1715 |

- **Solver round-trip**: identity (total, lossless).
- **Atlas round-trip**: only lossless where defined;

Tick 1714 (cron, 2026-06-04) — **Solver → Atlas →
Solver round-trip identity**: foundational
correspondence at the Solver/Atlas level.

Added in `Proofs/Adversarial.lean` right after
`Atlas.toSolver_apply_of_some`:

1. `Solver.toAtlas_toSolver`: for any solver σ,
   `σ.toAtlas.toSolver = σ` as functions. Proof:
   `funext _ _; rfl` — every step in the reduction
   chain is definitional.

**Proof analysis**: The chain
`σ.toAtlas.toSolver g p
   = (σ.toAtlas g p).getD _    -- defn of Atlas.toSolver
   = (some (σ g p)).getD _      -- defn of Solver.toAtlas
   = σ g p                       -- Option.getD pattern match`
collapses via three definitional reductions; `funext`
extends to function equality.

**Why substantive (per user pivot — Solver/Atlas
foundational correspondence)**:

This is the **left-inverse** of the
`Solver ↔ Atlas` correspondence:

- **Forward**: `Solver.toAtlas σ : Atlas` (always
  total, returning `some _`).
- **Backward**: `Atlas.toSolver A : Solver` (using
  `Option.getD` with default).
- **Round-trip 1** (this tick): `toSolver ∘ toAtlas
  = id` on solvers (identity).
- **Round-trip 2** (not yet proven, only partial):
  `toAtlas ∘ toSolver = id` only when atlas is
  total — generally `toAtlas (toSolver A)` differs
  from `A` at queries where `A` returns `none`.

The asymmetry reflects the fundamental difference:
solvers are TOTAL functions, atlases are PARTIAL
(`Option`-valued). Solvers embed into atlases via
`some`, but atlases project onto solvers via
`getD`.

**Goal-alignment**:
- (M4 — the Atlas): the Solver/Atlas
  correspondence has a clean round-trip identity
  on the solver side.
- (Atlas algebra): `Solver.toAtlas` is an
  **embedding** (left-injective; `toSolver` is its
  retraction).
- (Cycle/Atlas algebra): cycle solvers can be
  losslessly converted to atlases and back —
  foundational for the cycle ↔ atlas correspondence.

Proof structure: each of the four `IsClosedOn` fields splits
on `g = g₀ ∧ p = p₀` (decidable from `DecidableEq` on both):
- **Match case** (`obtain ⟨rfl, rfl⟩ := h`):
  - `total`: refined value is `some pl'`, `simp` closes via
    `Option.isSome_some`.
  - `valid`: extract `pl = pl'` via `Option.some.inj`,
    `subst`, then `⟨hpiece, hvalid⟩`.
  - `closed`: same extraction, then `hland`.
- **Non-match case**: forward to `hA.*` via `refine_apply_of_ne`.

The `not_lost` field doesn't case-split (states don't
change under refinement).

**Why substantive (per user pivot)**: third Atlas-algebra
primitive. Together with `restrict` and `unionOn`, the
algebra now supports:
- `restrict` — narrow the certified domain (Tick 1603);
- `unionOn` — expand by combining certificates (Tick 1604);
- `refine` — locally improve a single prescription (this tick).

These three primitives form a **minimal toolkit for
incremental Atlas construction**. Future M4 work can:
1. Start with a trivial single-state atlas;
2. Iteratively `unionOn` newly discovered closed sub-atlases;
3. `refine` weak prescriptions when a better placement is
   discovered;
4. `restrict` to the certified core when exporting.

**Note on admissibility**: `Atlas.IsClosedOn.refine` requires
the new placement to be admissible *unconditionally* (not
just when `g₀ ∈ S`). A weaker conditional form
(`g₀ ∈ S → ...`) would allow safer "no-op refinements" at
out-of-domain states, but the unconditional form is simpler
and suffices for the common use case (refining at a known
in-domain state).

**Goal-alignment**:
- (M4 — the Atlas): completes the trio of basic algebraic
  primitives needed for incremental construction.
- (M2/M3 — cycles): via Tick 1602's Iff, refinement pulls
  back to cycle-side: "swap a cycle solver's move at one
  state for another valid one that lands in the cycle".

Tick 1604 (cron, 2026-06-03) — **second Atlas-algebra
operation**: `Atlas.unionOn` with priority dispatch +
closure preservation.

Added in `Proofs/Adversarial.lean`:

1. `Atlas.unionOn A B S₁ S₂ : Atlas cfg` — combine two
   atlases: if `g ∈ S₁` use `A g p`, else if `g ∈ S₂` use
   `B g p`, else `none`. **Priority dispatch** (`A` wins on
   overlap) eliminates the need for a disjointness
   hypothesis.
2. Three apply-form lemmas:
   - `unionOn_apply_of_mem_left` — `g ∈ S₁ → union = A g p`;
   - `unionOn_apply_of_mem_right` — `g ∉ S₁ ∧ g ∈ S₂ → union = B g p`;
   - `unionOn_apply_of_notMem` — `g ∉ S₁ ∧ g ∉ S₂ → union = none`.
3. `Atlas.IsClosedOn.unionOn` — **closure preservation**:
   `A.IsClosedOn cfg S₁ → B.IsClosedOn cfg S₂ →
    (A.unionOn B S₁ S₂).IsClosedOn cfg (S₁ ∪ S₂)`.

Proof structure: each of the four `IsClosedOn` fields splits
on `g ∈ S₁` vs `g ∈ S₂ \ S₁` via `by_cases h₁ : g ∈ S₁` +
`hg.resolve_left h₁`. The `not_lost` field doesn't need
the case split (both atlases cover their side). The
`closed` field uses `Finset.mem_union_left` /
`mem_union_right` to land back in `S₁ ∪ S₂`.

     piece;

   a closed Atlas on the reachable subgraph IS a

   domain.

   language, is `Atlas.IsClosedOn` its state set. Proof:
   field-by-field forwarding of cycle invariants via
   `simp [Solver.toAtlas]` + `Option.some.injEq`.

Tick 1599 (cron, 2026-06-03): proved
`AdversarialClosedCycle.init_image_bag_card_ge_two`
in `Proofs/SafeIterateFinite.lean` — the **unconditional
bag-diversity lower bound** for init cycles.

Statement: `init ∈ C.states → 2 ≤ |image bag|`.

Proof: `init.bag = Bag.full` (card 7) is in the image. By
`closed`, the successor `g'` of `init` under `Piece.O` (or
any piece) is also in the cycle; its bag is
`Bag.full.draw Piece.O`, which differs from `Bag.full`
(card 6 vs 7, by `Bag.draw_full_ne_full`). So the image
contains two distinct bags. Close via `Finset.one_lt_card.mpr`
on the two explicit witnesses.

Pivoted from the originally planned symmetric corollary
(`single-bag-cycle → 28 ≤ image board`) because this gives
**strictly more**: it shows the symmetric hypothesis
`|image bag| ≤ 1` is *impossible* for init cycles. The
single-bag corollary would have been vacuously useful;
this unconditional lower bound is the actual structural
fact.

One linter touch-up: `show` → `change`.

**Why substantive (per user pivot)**: an unconditional
structural fact about init-cycle topology. Combined with
Ticks 1593, 1598:
- `|image bag| ≥ 2` always (this tick);
- `|image bag| ≤ 128` always (Tick 1590);
- `|C.states| ∈ [28, |image board| * |image bag|]` (Ticks
  1591-1597).

Notable **asymmetry**: `|image board| ≥ 2` is *false* in
general (line-clearing can return to empty board), but
`|image bag| ≥ 2` is forced (bag strictly shrinks after
init's first draw). The bag dimension is the *honest*
diversity dimension.

**Goal-alignment**:
- (Goal 1 — adversarial cycle): rules out *trivial* cycles
  with constant bag. Any valid init cycle must traverse at
  least two distinct bag states — a real dynamical
  constraint, not just an enumeration artifact.

expression that the trace is a function of the past, not the
future — the standard definition of *non-anticipative
dynamics*. Pivoted from the planned "LegalSequence
periodicity" because identifying the canonical 7-bag
alignment requires substantial new bag-cycle theory.
`adversarialTrace_congr` is shorter, foundational, and
unlocks easier reasoning about sequence modifications.

**Goal-alignment**:
- (Goal 1 — adversarial cycle): direct usefulness for
  arguments that *modify* a piece sequence beyond some
  cutoff (e.g., to construct a sequence that loops with
  shorter period than `|inFieldStates|`) — the prefix is
  guaranteed unaffected.
- (Foundational): the policy/solver outputs at index `< n`
  cannot depend on `s k` for `k ≥ n`, formalised
  rigorously.

Tick 1566 (cron, 2026-06-03): added
`adversarialTrace_iterated_period_of_periodic_suffix` in
`Proofs/Adversarial.lean` — iterates Tick 1565's single-period
shift to give honest lattice periodicity.

Statement: under the same hypotheses as Tick 1565
(trace recurrence `trace b = trace (b + d)` AND sequence
periodicity `s (b + k) = s (b + d + k)`), for every `n : ℕ`:
`trace s g0 (b + n * d) = trace s g0 b`.

Proof: induction on `n`. Base = `simp` (since `b + 0*d = b`).
Step uses Tick 1565 at offset `k * d` to get
`trace (b + k*d) = trace (b + d + k*d)`, then rewrites
`b + d + k*d = b + (k+1)*d` by `ring` and closes with IH.

**Why substantive (per user pivot)**: this completes the
periodicity chain `add → single-period → lattice-period`.
The trace is now provably constant on the arithmetic lattice
`{b + n*d | n ∈ ℕ}` whenever both hypotheses hold — a real
dynamical-systems result on the adversarial system.

**Goal-alignment**:
- (Goal 1 — adversarial cycle): an *infinite* set of trace
  indices map to the same state, by a closed-form arithmetic
  index. This is the structural ingredient for the M3 proof
  obligation "an init-reachable cycle implies infinite play":
  if `trace b ∈ C.states` and the period closes, then
  `trace (b + n*d) ∈ C.states` for all `n`, including `n`
  large enough to outrun any termination bound.

Tick 1565 (cron, 2026-06-03): added
`adversarialTrace_periodic_of_periodic_suffix` in
`Proofs/Adversarial.lean` — the first true **periodicity
theorem** on the adversarial trace.

Statement: if the trace has a recurrence at `(b, b + d)`
(`trace s g0 b = trace s g0 (b + d)`) AND the piece sequence
is `d`-periodic on `[b, ∞)` (`s (b + k) = s (b + d + k)` for
all `k`), then the entire trace suffix is `d`-periodic:
`trace s g0 (b + k) = trace s g0 (b + d + k)` for all `k`.

Proof: factor both `trace s g0 (b + k)` and
`trace s g0 (b + d + k)` via `adversarialTrace_add` (Tick
1564), rewrite by the recurrence hypothesis to unify starting
states, then `funext` on the two time-shifted piece sequences
(equal pointwise by `hs`).

**Why substantive (per user pivot)**: this isn't a card
companion — it's a real dynamical-systems-style result on the
adversarial system. The two hypotheses are both essential:
- the *trace* recurrence alone doesn't give periodicity
  (the future depends on the input sequence);
- the *sequence* periodicity alone doesn't give trace
  periodicity (different starting states diverge).

**Goal-alignment**:
- (Goal 1 — adversarial cycle): the foundational
  periodicity result. Combined with M2/M3 pigeonhole, the
  next step is to specialise to `LegalSequence`'s natural
  7-periodicity inside the bag-cycle, giving a route from
  "pigeonhole recurrence" to "honest periodic trace".

Tick 1564 (cron, 2026-06-03): added `adversarialTrace_add`
in `Proofs/Adversarial.lean` — a **foundational
compositional identity** on the adversarial trace.

Statement: `adversarialTrace cfg σ s g0 (n + m)
  = adversarialTrace cfg σ (fun k => s (n + k))
      (adversarialTrace cfg σ s g0 n) m`.

I.e. running for `n + m` steps = running for `n` steps to
reach the intermediate state, then running for `m` more steps
under the **time-shifted** piece sequence. Analogue of
`Survival.trace_add` for adversarial play.

Proof: induction on `m`; `zero` case is `rfl`; `succ` case
reshapes `n + (k+1) = (n+k) + 1` and applies
`adversarialTrace_succ` on both sides plus IH — closes by
`rfl` because the inner state, piece argument, and solver
output all agree definitionally.

**Why substantive (per user pivot)**: this is the
compositional law that lets you reason about long traces in
terms of intermediate snapshots. Pivoted away from
standard/tiny specialisation churn — `adversarialTrace_add`
unlocks:
- proving that if `trace s g0 b = trace s g0 (b + d)` AND the
  piece sequence is `d`-periodic on `[b, ∞)`, then the trace
  is `d`-periodic on `[b, ∞)`;
- splitting any trace-based argument at an arbitrary
  intermediate step;
- composing cycle-entry and in-cycle reasoning.

**Goal-alignment**:
- (Goal 1 — adversarial cycle): foundational toolkit
  enabling true periodicity proofs (not just one-step
  recurrences).

`AdversarialClosedCycle.adversarialTrace_pigeonhole_via_inFieldStates_of_init`

Tick 103 (cron, 2026-05-31): added `ValidSolver` and `SolvesTetrisValid`
in `Proofs/Adversarial.lean`:

```
def ValidSolver (cfg) (σ) : Prop :=
  ∀ g p, p ∈ g.bag → (σ g p).piece = p ∧ (σ g p).Valid cfg

def SolvesTetrisValid (cfg) (σ) : Prop :=
  ValidSolver cfg σ ∧ SolvesTetris cfg σ
```

`SolvesTetris` alone is too permissive: it doesn't require the solver's
placements to be in-bounds, only that the resulting trace doesn't lose.
This obstructs the harder direction of `TetrisSolvable ↔ init ∈ safe`
(because `safe` requires *valid* placements). `SolvesTetrisValid` is the
strengthened version that aligns with `safe`. Build passes, both
axiom-clean, 0 sorries.

0 sorries. Next: `AdversarialClosedCycle.cycle_state_wf` — discharge the
WF hypothesis directly from the cycle structure (currently a free
hypothesis in `cycle_subset_inFieldStates_of_wf`). The proof needs a
chain-like induction: every cycle state must be reachable from *some*
WF state in the cycle, and `applyStep_wf` plus the cycle's `valid`
obligation preserves WF along chains.

**Subtlety**: the cycle's `closed` obligation doesn't say states are
*reachable from `init`* through cycle moves — it only says successors stay
in the cycle. So we can't simply argue "init → ... → s preserves WF". We'd
need to either (a) add a `Reachable` invariant to the structure, or
(b) prove that a non-WF cycle state implies a contradiction via some other
invariant, or (c) restrict attention to "init-cycles" where states are
defined as the forward-reachable closure from init.

Tick 64 (cron, 2026-05-30): proved `init_states_card_ge_twenty_eight {cfg}
(C) (h : init ∈ C.states) : 28 ≤ C.states.card`. The first **biUnion-based**
cycle-size bound, using all the infrastructure from Ticks 60-63:

```
S := insert init ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 6)).biUnion (C.chainLayer h))
```

Proof skeleton:
1. `chainLayer h` is `PairwiseDisjoint` on `Finset.univ.toSet` (Tick 63).
2. `Finset.card_biUnion hpair` reduces to a sum `∑ k : Fin 6, (chainLayer
   k).card`.
3. `Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun k _ => C.chainLayer_card h k)` rewrites the
   summand to `7 - k.val`.
4. `decide` evaluates `∑ k : Fin 6, (7 - k.val) = 27`.
5. `Finset.card_insert_of_notMem (C.init_notMem_chainLayer_∃_k ...)` adds 1.

One `show` → `change` linter fix. Build passes with one deprecation note
about `Finset.toSet` (signature change in mathlib — purely informational).
Axiom-clean, 0 sorries. **Lower bound on init-cycles raised from 14 → 28.**
Pattern is now fully indexed: extending to depth-7 (the full bag refill
cycle) requires more care about overlap. Next: either (A) prove
`init_states_card_ge_twenty_nine` by adding the depth-6 chain state (which
has bag.card = 1, distinguishable from all layers) — note this requires
showing chain states are distinct from layer elements; or (B) start work
on degenerate-config solvability (1.2 from ROADMAP: pick a tiny config
where a concrete `AdversarialClosedCycle` is feasible to construct).

  via `card_draw_of_ge_two`. Size 6.

Tick 51 (cron, 2026-05-30): proved `AdversarialClosedCycle.states_card_gt_bag_card

## Next sub-task (pick this when you start the next tick)

**1.2 deeper: explore lower bounds on `states.card` from bag-cycle length.**

We have ≥ 2. The 7-bag forces stronger lower bounds: any cycle must contain
states for at least 7 distinct bag-arrangements (every piece is drawn at
least once per bag, and the bag at each state evolves deterministically under
the solver's chosen draws). The actual lower bound depends on how the cycle
intersects the bag-state graph.

Two atomic next steps:

**Option A**: prove that any cycle containing some `s` must contain a chain
`s → s.step → s.step.step → …` of length at least `s.bag.card`, since each
step removes one piece from the bag until it refills. After `s.bag.card`
steps the bag is empty (then refills). So `states.card ≥ s.bag.card`.

Statement: `AdversarialClosedCycle.states_card_ge_bag_card {cfg} (C) {s} (hs)
: s.bag.card ≤ C.states.card`.

**Option B**: prove `states.card ≥ 7` for cycles containing `init` (which has
`bag = Bag.full`, `card = 7`).

Recommended: Option A is the more general fact; B is a corollary with `init`
substituted.

Both require a chain-construction (iterate `closed` several times). Likely
a `Finset.range`-based image argument: map `n : Fin s.bag.card` to the state
after `n` solver-driven steps from `s` (using a sequence of pieces drawn from
the bag), prove all are distinct via cardinality drop on each step.

- **2.11b**: `safe → WF` is NOT obvious from the current `safe` definition.
  `safe_not_lost` gives `∀ p ∈ b, p.2 < cfg.rows` (in-field rows), but
  out-of-bounds columns aren't excluded. Need either to redefine
  `safe`/`safeOp` to require WF inputs, or define `inFieldStates` without
  the WF requirement (use a `Finset (Fin rows-bounded board × Bag)` rather
  than the existing `InFieldBoard`). Either approach has implications;
  needs design choice before proceeding.

### Tick (manual, 2026-08-23x) — the balance theorem: 5 of each piece per period (bank 20/N)

**`window_thirtyfive_balanced`** (BagCadence): a 35-draw window with equal bag
states at both ends — every closed-cycle period — deals **every piece exactly
five times**. Proof by the counting trick (no uniqueness bookkeeping):
- `mem_bagAt_succ_of_ne` / `mem_bagAt_of_not_drawn` — a piece not drawn
  survives (erase keeps it; refill restores it).
- `bagAt_full_iterate` — refills every 7 from a refill.
- Lower bound 5 per piece: one hit in the head (drains the current bag) OR
  the tail (else the piece would survive to the equal end bag), plus one in
  each of four full blocks.
- Total = 35 (`Finset.card_eq_sum_card_fiberwise`) and 7 × 5 = 35 forces
  equality (sum-split with `Finset.sum_ite_eq'`).

Consequences queued: #T = 5k per cycle period (the charge-theory input);
#I = 5k ⇒ tetris count ≤ 5k per period.

**MAJOR proof-engineering find:** `bagAt`'s `draw` duplicates its argument in
the ite condition AND branch, so any whnf at a symbolic offset (n + 35)
doubles the term per layer — exponential (1M+ `Finset.val` unfolds; found via
`set_option diagnostics true`). Fix: `attribute [local irreducible] bagAt` in
a section around the theorem — every proof step uses opaque lemmas anyway.
Record for ALL future bagAt-heavy proofs.

### Tick (manual, 2026-08-23g) — the stationary lag profile (bank expansion 3/N)

The last statistical stone. `ClearDeviation` additions:
- **`sum_grid_gap_eq`** — pure double-sum algebra: `∑∑ γ(|i−j|)` over the L×L
  grid = `L·γ(0) + 2·∑_{l=1}^{L−1} (L−l)·γ(l)`. Induction on L peeling the new
  row+column; `Finset.sum_range_reflect` handles the reversal.
- **`stationary_covariance_budget`** — if the covariances depend only on the
  lag (`cov(Xᵢ, Xᵢ₊ₗ) = γ(l)`), bounded partial sums cap the whole weighted
  lag profile: `L·γ(0) + 2·∑ (L−l)·γ(l) ≤ B²`. This is exactly Var(S_L) under
  stationarity, so it packages `covariance_sum_le` into the standard
  time-series object.
- **`survival_stationary_lag_budget`** — the game instance with B = 20:
  `L·γ(0) + 2·∑ (L−l)·γ(l) ≤ 400` for every horizon. Divide by L: the
  spectral density at zero of an immortal solver's clear series vanishes at
  rate O(1/L), with the negative lags obligated to cancel γ(0).

### Tick (manual, 2026-08-23d) — standing inventory: the occupancy FLOOR

New statistical property of the ideal solver: survival forces a LOWER bound on
time-averaged board occupancy. **NEW**
`proofs/Proofs/Survival/StandingInventory.lean` (green, no warnings):
- `sumCount π n` — cumulative occupancy over the first `n` checkpoints.
- `six_le_count_of_clearing` — every clearing moment sits on ≥ 6 banked cells
  (a `k`-clear needs `10k − 4`).
- `ten_cleared_le_sumCount` — the banked-mass ledger: summing the per-clear
  requirement, `10·cleared ≤ ∑count + 4·clearingSteps`.
- **`standing_inventory_floor`** — `12n ≤ 5·∑count + 1000`: the time-averaged
  occupancy of ANY surviving play is ≥ `2.4 − 200/n` cells. Derivation:
  clearing duty ≥ 0.4 rows/piece (floor) + each clear needs banked mass +
  clearing moments ≤ 0.4n. A singles-only sawtooth achieves average 4, so the
  floor is within 2× of achievable. **Empty-board play is impossible.**
- **`card_empty_times_le`** — `5·#{t<n | board empty} ≤ n+4`: the board can be
  empty only at `5 ∣ t` (residue clock), so an immortal solver's board is
  **occupied ≥ 80% of the time**, even for a perfect-clear-loop strategy.

### Tick (manual, 2026-08-22b) — the clear-size mix is free

Question: must a surviving player use singles/doubles/triples/tetrises in some
forced proportion?

**Answer: no.** **NEW** `proofs/Proofs/Survival/ClearMix.lean` (green, no
warnings, base-axiom-clean):
- `sizeCount cfg π g0 k n` — drops among the first `n` clearing exactly `k`
  rows; `iCount` — drops playing an I.
- **`mix_identity`**: `a₁ + 2a₂ + 3a₃ + 4a₄ = cleared` (every cleared row belongs
  to exactly one drop; `fullRows_card_le_four` makes the four sizes exhaustive).
- **`mix_law`**: `10·(a₁+2a₂+3a₃+4a₄) + occupancy = 4·pieces`. **One linear
  equation in four unknowns ⇒ three degrees of freedom ⇒ NO proportion is
  forced.** Per bag: `f₁+2f₂+3f₃+4f₄ = 2.8`, all four corners available
  (singles 2.8/bag = 40% of pieces, doubles 1.4, triples 14/15, tetrises 0.7).
- Corners made sharp: **`tetris_only_count_ge`** (`28m ≤ 40a₄ + 200`, i.e. a
  tetris-only player must tetris in ≥`0.7m − 5` bags — 70% of all bags, lifetime
  slack five) and `singles_only_count_ge` (`28m ≤ 10a₁ + 200`).
- The one genuine side-constraint: **`sizeCount_four_le_iCount`** — only I spans
  four rows (`tetris_requires_I`), so `a₄ ≤ #I` and a bag admits ≤1 tetris. It
  does **not** bind asymptotically: `ten_mul_sizeCount_four_le` gives
  `10a₄ ≤ n` from the rate alone, tighter than the I supply `n/7`. That
  non-collision is exactly why the tetris corner is arithmetically reachable.

Recorded negative (module docstring): arithmetic admits every mix but constructs
none. Whether a mix is *playable* is geometry. The content is that **no counting
argument will ever rule a mix out** — any obstruction to a pure strategy must be
structural.
